Diffusion-State Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion Language Models

Daisuke Oba Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan Correspondence to: daisuke.oba@nlp.comp.isct.ac.jp    Hiroki Furuta Affiliation: Tokyo, Japan    Naoaki Okazaki Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan
Abstract

Masked diffusion language models generate by iteratively filling masked tokens over multiple denoising steps, so learning only from a terminal reward on the final completion yields coarse credit assignment over intermediate decisions. We propose DiSPO (Diffusion-State Policy Optimization), a plug-in credit-assignment layer that directly optimizes intermediate filling decisions. At selected intermediate masked states, DiSPO branches by resampling fillings for the currently masked positions from rollout-cached logits, scores the resulting completions, and updates only the newly filled tokens—without additional multi-step diffusion rollouts. We formalize a fixed-state objective for branched completions and derive a policy-gradient estimator that can be combined with terminal-feedback policy optimization using the same rollouts. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, DiSPO consistently improves over the terminal-feedback diffu-GRPO baseline on math and planning benchmarks under matched rollout compute and optimizer steps. Our code will be available at https://daioba.github.io/dispo.

Keywords: 
Diffusion Language Models, Reinforcement Learning

1 Introduction

Policy optimization (PO) is a standard tool for improving the reasoning and alignment behavior of language models, spanning preference-based RLHF (Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022) and policy-gradient methods (Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017), including recent PPO-style variants for reasoning (Shao et al., 2024). Most PO setups, however, rely on a scalar reward computed on the final completion and broadcast it uniformly across tokens, which yields coarse credit assignment.

This limitation is especially acute for masked diffusion language models (MDLMs), which generate by repeatedly filling masked positions over multiple denoising steps (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2025). Early fillings constrain what can be fixed later, so success depends on a sequence of intermediate decisions. Recent work goes beyond purely terminal feedback, e.g., via reward shaping based on intermediate states or trajectory-level comparisons at fixed steps (Xie et al., 2025; He et al., 2025). Our key difference is the optimization unit: instead of optimizing over denoising trajectories, we optimize state-conditioned mask fillings by holding an intermediate masked sequence fixed and resampling alternative fillings.

To address this gap, we propose DiSPO (Diffusion-State Policy Optimization; Fig. 1), a plug-in credit-assignment layer that optimizes intermediate filling decisions via fixed-state comparisons (§ 3). Motivated by the policy-gradient formulation (Williams, 1992; Sutton et al., 1999), we treat a partially-masked sequence as the state and the token assignments to its masked positions as the action. At selected intermediate states, DiSPO resamples multiple candidate fillings from rollout-cached logits, forms draft completions, evaluates the same terminal reward, and updates only the newly filled tokens. Because each denoising step outputs distributions for all masked positions, this branching reuses rollout logits and requires no additional multi-step diffusion rollouts. DiSPO is modular and can be trained jointly with standard terminal-feedback policy optimization (Alg. 1).

We formalize a fixed-state expected-return objective for intermediate-state branching and show that DiSPO yields a valid policy-gradient estimator for it (Theorem 4.1). Moreover, the step-wise update reuses the same rollouts as terminal-feedback policy optimization (Fig. 1), so the two objectives can be optimized jointly as a single mixed objective in expectation (Theorem 4.2). Finally, restricting updates to newly filled tokens and averaging over same-state branches reduces variance in step-wise gradient (Propositions 4.3 and 4.4).

We evaluate DiSPO on LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) under the same terminal-feedback training recipe used in prior MDLM policy optimization (Zhao et al., 2025b). For a controlled comparison, we match the dominant training costs—multi-step diffusion rollouts and optimizer update steps—so improvements reflect finer state-conditioned credit assignment rather than extra rollouts. Across math reasoning (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023)) and symbolic planning (Sudoku and Countdown (Zhao et al., 2025b)), DiSPO yields consistent gains. Ablations attribute these gains to same-state branching and updating only newly filled tokens (§ 5.4).

In the following, we provide background in §2, present DiSPO in §3, analyze it in §4, report experiments in §5, and review related work in §6.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Terminal-feedback policy optimization for LMs

We view a language model as a conditional policy πθ​(o∣q)\pi_{\theta}(o\mid q) over completions oo given a prompt qq. In terminal-feedback policy optimization, a scalar reward R⁡(q,o)R(q,o) is evaluated on the final completion, and learning updates are driven by likelihood-ratio (policy-gradient) objectives at the sequence level. This bandit-style view is broadly applicable, but it attributes the same terminal signal to all decoding decisions, yielding coarse credit assignment.

A common instantiation is group-based policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024). Given GG sampled completions o1,…,oG∼πθold(⋅∣q)o_{1},\dots,o_{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid q) and terminal rewards ri=R⁡(q,oi)r_{i}=R(q,o_{i}), define the group baseline r¯=1G​∑i=1Gri\bar{r}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}r_{i} and advantages Ai=ri−r¯A_{i}=r_{i}-\bar{r}. A concise likelihood-ratio objective (optionally with a KL penalty to a reference policy πref\pi_{\text{ref}}) is

𝔼q[1G∑i=1Gπθ​(oi∣q)πθold​(oi∣q)⏟ρi​(θ)Ai−βKL(πθ(⋅∣q)∥πref(⋅∣q))].\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\underbrace{\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}\mid q)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{i}\mid q)}}_{\rho_{i}(\theta)}\,A_{i}\!-\!\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid q)\right)\right].

We use this terminal-feedback formulation as a convenient baseline and as a plug-in component for our method.

2.2 Surrogate likelihood for terminal-feedback optimization of MDLMs

Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively refining a partially-masked sequence, unmasking tokens in an arbitrary order. This makes the exact sequence likelihood log⁡πθ​(o∣q)\log\pi_{\theta}(o\!\mid\!q) intractable, which prevents directly applying standard terminal-feedback objectives such as § 2.1. To enable terminal-feedback policy optimization for MDLMs, Zhao et al. (2025b) introduces a tractable surrogate likelihood π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} (yielding an MDLM instantiation often referred to as diffu-GRPO).

Given a prompt–completion pair (q,o)(q,o), we sample a random prompt-masking pattern mm to obtain a corrupted prompt q(m)q^{(m)}. We then form a fully masked completion o~\tilde{o}, run a single denoising step to obtain per-position token distributions pθ(⋅∣q(m),o~)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q^{(m)},\tilde{o}), and define the surrogate log-probability

log⁡π~θ​(o∣q)=𝔼m​[∑j=1|o|log⁡pθ​(oj∣q(m),o~)].\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(o\mid q)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{m}\!\left[\;\sum_{j=1}^{|o|}\log p_{\theta}\!\bigl(o_{j}\mid q^{(m)},\tilde{o}\bigr)\;\right]. (1)

In terminal-feedback MDLM policy optimization, π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} replaces πθ\pi_{\theta} inside likelihood ratios and KL terms, allowing MDLMs to be trained as conditional policies from scalar rewards on final completions.

2.3 Rethinking MDLM decision points for RL

In an episodic MDP, the policy gradient theorem (Williams, 1992; Sutton et al., 1999) states that for a stochastic policy πθ​(at∣st)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}),

∇θJ​(θ)=𝔼⁡[∑t∇θ​log​πθ​(at∣st)​Gt],\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\,G_{t}\right],

where sts_{t} and ata_{t} are the state and action, and GtG_{t} denotes the return from step tt. Each decision (st,at)(s_{t},a_{t}) contributes an explicit term ∇θ​log​πθ​(at∣st)​Gt\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\!\mid\!s_{t})\,G_{t}. This decomposition enables fine-grained credit assignment across steps.

Most RL formulations for LMs (autoregressive or diffusion) collapse decoding to a terminal-reward bandit, where reward evaluation and gradient attribution are both driven by the final completion (Shao et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025b). MDLMs, however, provide an anytime completion interface: at an intermediate masked state, a single forward pass yields logits for all masked positions. Hence we can view the masked sequence as the state sts_{t} and its mask fillings as the action ata_{t}; filling deterministically yields a completion to score with the same terminal reward, and cached logits enable multiple same-state counterfactual completions without additional rollout forward passes. This state–action view motivates our diffusion-state policy optimization in §3.

3 Diffusion-State Policy Optimization

In this section, we propose Diffusion-State Policy Optimization (DiSPO), which performs policy optimization at intermediate diffusion states of MDLMs. At selected partially-masked states, DiSPO resamples mask fillings from rollout-cached logits to form same-state counterfactual completions, scores them with the same terminal reward, and backpropagates gradients only through the newly filled tokens—without additional rollout forward passes. DiSPO is a plug-in credit-assignment layer composable with any terminal-feedback objective; in this paper we instantiate the terminal term with diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b). Algo. 1 summarizes the training procedure.

3.1 RL Formulation

States. For a prompt q∼𝒟q\!\sim\!\mathcal{D} and behavior parameters θold\theta_{\text{old}}, a multi-step MDLM sampler produces a trajectory of partially-masked sequences xk,1,xk,2,…,xk,Tx_{k,1},x_{k,2},\dots,x_{k,T}, where TT is the number of denoising steps and kk indexes trajectories. Each xk,t∈(𝒱∪{[MASK]})Lx_{k,t}\!\in\!(\mathcal{V}\!\cup\!\{\texttt{[MASK]}\})^{L} is a length-LL sequence with a subset of positions masked. Let

Mk,t={i:xk,t,i=[MASK]},Uk,t=[L]∖Mk,t,M_{k,t}=\{i:\,x_{k,t,i}=\texttt{[MASK]}\},\quad U_{k,t}=[L]\setminus M_{k,t},

and define the diffusion state at step tt as sk,t=(q,xk,t)s_{k,t}=(q,x_{k,t}).

Actions and policy factorization. At state sk,ts_{k,t}, the MDLM outputs logits for all i∈Mk,ti\in M_{k,t}, inducing per-position token distributions πθ(⋅∣sk,t,i)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t},i). We define the action as the joint filling of the currently masked positions, ak,t={ak,t,i}i∈Mk,ta_{k,t}=\{a_{k,t,i}\}_{i\in M_{k,t}}, with the factorized policy

πθ​(ak,t∣sk,t)=∏i∈Mk,tπθ​(ak,t,i∣sk,t,i).\pi_{\theta}(a_{k,t}\mid s_{k,t})\;=\;\prod_{i\in M_{k,t}}\pi_{\theta}\bigl(a_{k,t,i}\mid s_{k,t},i\bigr). (2)

Applying an action yields a completion deterministically: o=Fill​(xk,t,ak,t)o=\textsc{Fill}(x_{k,t},a_{k,t}), which replaces xk,t,ix_{k,t,i} by ak,t,ia_{k,t,i} for i∈Mk,ti\in M_{k,t} and keeps Uk,tU_{k,t} fixed. This state–action view makes it natural to evaluate intermediate decisions using the same terminal reward R⁡(q,o)R(q,o). Moreover, DiSPO attributes gradients only to the action distribution πθ​(ak,t∣sk,t)\pi_{\theta}(a_{k,t}\mid s_{k,t}), i.e., the newly filled tokens on Mk,tM_{k,t}, treating previously filled tokens as part of the state. In practice, likelihood ratios and KL terms are computed with a tractable masked-token surrogate introduced in § 3.3.

3.2 Per-state Branching and Rewards

For each prompt q∼𝒟q\!\sim\!\mathcal{D}, we first sample KK behavior trajectories by running the multi-step MDLM sampler with frozen parameters θold\theta_{\text{old}}, obtaining {xk,1:T}k=1K\{x_{k,1:T}\}_{k=1}^{K} and terminal completions ok=xk,To_{k}\!=\!x_{k,T}. During rollout, we cache the logits for each masked position i∈Mk,ti\!\in\!M_{k,t} at every visited state sk,ts_{k,t}.

We then select a set of state indices 𝒮⊆{(k,t)}\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{(k,t)\} to update. For each selected (k,t)∈𝒮(k,t)\in\mathcal{S}, we form a state-conditioned group by branching from the state: using cached logits at sk,ts_{k,t}, we resample ZZ actions

ak,t,1,…,ak,t,Z∼πθold(⋅∣sk,t)=∏i∈Mk,tπθold(⋅∣sk,t,i),a_{k,t,1},\dots,a_{k,t,Z}\!\sim\!\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t})\!=\!\prod_{i\in M_{k,t}}\!\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t},i),

and obtain completions ok,t,z=Fill​(xk,t,ak,t,z)o_{k,t,z}\!=\!\textsc{Fill}(x_{k,t},a_{k,t,z}). Since branching reuses rollout-cached logits, generating these ZZ completions incurs no additional rollout forward passes.

Each completion is scored by the same terminal reward function,

Rk,t,z=R⁡(q,ok,t,z),R_{k,t,z}=R(q,o_{k,t,z}),

and we compute a per-state baseline and group-relative advantages:

R¯k,t=1Z​∑z=1ZRk,t,z,Ak,t,z=Rk,t,z−R¯k,t.\bar{R}_{k,t}=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}R_{k,t,z},\quad A_{k,t,z}=R_{k,t,z}-\bar{R}_{k,t}. (3)

These advantages capture state-conditioned preferences over alternative fillings under a fixed intermediate state.

3.3 Step-level Surrogate Log-probabilities

To optimize masked-token actions at intermediate states, we need tractable log-probabilities to form likelihood ratios for the diffusion-state policy. Following Zhao et al. (2025b), we use a one-step masked-token surrogate π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} (Eq. 1), and adapt it to a state-wise definition that accounts only for the currently masked positions.

State-wise masked-token surrogate. For each state sk,t=(q,xk,t)s_{k,t}=(q,x_{k,t}), sample a random prompt-masking pattern mm to obtain a corrupted prompt q(m)q^{(m)} and define sk,t(m)=(q(m),xk,t)s_{k,t}^{(m)}\!=\!(q^{(m)},x_{k,t}). Running a single denoising step on sk,t(m)s_{k,t}^{(m)} yields per-position distributions π~θ(⋅∣sk,t(m),i)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t}^{(m)},i) for all i∈Mk,ti\in M_{k,t}. For an action sample ak,t,za_{k,t,z}, define the state-wise surrogate log-probability by summing over actionable positions:

log⁡π~θ​(ak,t,z∣sk,t):=𝔼m​[∑i∈Mk,tlog⁡π~θ​(ak,t,z,i∣sk,t(m),i)].\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{k,t,z}\!\mid\!s_{k,t})\!:=\!\mathbb{E}_{m}\!\!\left[\sum_{i\in M_{k,t}}\!\!\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}\bigl(a_{k,t,z,i}\!\mid\!s_{k,t}^{(m)}\!,\!i\bigr)\right]. (4)

This restriction makes the update token-local: rewards computed from completions affect only the newly filled tokens at the current state.

Implementation note. We estimate the expectation over mm with the same Monte Carlo scheme as Zhao et al. (2025b). All log-probabilities, likelihood ratios, and KL terms in our objectives are computed using π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}.

3.4 Training Objective

For clarity, we present the unclipped likelihood-ratio objectives; our implementation uses standard clipping and a KL penalty to a reference surrogate policy π~ref\tilde{\pi}_{\text{ref}}.

State-wise objective. For each selected state (k,t)∈𝒮(k,t)\in\mathcal{S}, we have ZZ action samples with rewards {(ak,t,z,Rk,t,z)}z=1Z\{(a_{k,t,z},R_{k,t,z})\}_{z=1}^{Z} and advantages from Eq. 3. Using the state-wise surrogate (Eq. 4), define the likelihood ratio

ρk,t,z​(θ)=exp⁡(log⁡π~θ​(ak,t,z∣sk,t)−log⁡π~θold​(ak,t,z∣sk,t)).\rho_{k,t,z}(\theta)\!=\!\exp\!\Bigl(\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{k,t,z}\!\mid\!s_{k,t})-\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{k,t,z}\!\mid\!s_{k,t})\Bigr).

The step-level loss at (k,t)(k,t) is

ℒstep(k,t)(θ)=−1Z∑z=1Zρk,t,z(θ)Ak,t,z,\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(k,t)}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{Z}\sum\nolimits_{z=1}^{Z}\rho_{k,t,z}(\theta)\,A_{k,t,z}, (5)

and the aggregated step-level loss is

ℒstep​(θ)=∑(k,t)∈𝒮ℒstep(k,t)​(θ).{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)}=\sum\nolimits_{(k,t)\in\mathcal{S}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(k,t)}(\theta). (6)

Terminal objective. The step-wise objective can be combined with any terminal-feedback policy-optimization objective on final completions. In this paper, for controlled comparison, we instantiate it with diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b). For each prompt qq, rollout completions {ok}k=1K\{o_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} are scored by rk=R⁡(q,ok)r_{k}=R(q,o_{k}) and converted to group-relative advantages using r¯q=1K​∑k=1Krk\bar{r}_{q}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_{k}. Using the sequence-level surrogate log-probabilities log⁡π~θ​(q,ok)\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(q,o_{k}) (Eq. 1), define

ρk​(θ)=exp⁡(log⁡π~θ​(q,ok)−log⁡π~θold​(q,ok)),\rho_{k}(\theta)=\exp\!\Bigl(\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(q,o_{k})-\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(q,o_{k})\Bigr),

The terminal loss is

ℒterm(θ)=−1K∑k=1Kρk(θ)Ak.{\color[rgb]{0.21,0.12,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)}=-\frac{1}{K}\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}(\theta)\,A_{k}. (7)

Combined objective. We optimize a weighted combination of step-wise and terminal objectives:

ℒ⁡(θ)=αterm​ℒterm​(θ)+αstep​ℒstep​(θ),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\alpha_{\text{term}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.21,0.12,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)}+\alpha_{\text{step}}\,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)}, (8)

where αstep,αterm∈ℝ≥0\alpha_{\text{step}},\alpha_{\text{term}}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. We set αterm=1\alpha_{\text{term}}\!=\!1 in experiments.

4 Theoretical Analysis

DiSPO treats intermediate diffusion states as decision points and directly optimizes their mask fillings via policy gradients. Under the masked-token surrogate policy π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} (Eq. 4), we show that the step-wise loss provides a principled policy-gradient estimator for a fixed-state objective (Theorem 4.1). We further show that combining step-wise and terminal losses corresponds in expectation to optimizing a single objective (Theorem 4.2). We also provide simple variance-reduction mechanisms that justify token-local updates and same-state averaging (§4.3). For clarity, we analyze the unclipped likelihood-ratio objective without KL.

4.1 Step-wise Objective and Step-level Policy Gradient

Fix a denoising step index tt. Let dt​(q)d_{t}(q) denote the distribution over intermediate states at step tt induced by rolling out the frozen behavior model θold\theta_{\text{old}} on prompts q∼𝒟q\sim\mathcal{D}. Using the state–action view in §3.1, define

Jt(θ):=𝔼q∼𝒟𝔼st∼dt​(q)𝔼a∼π~θ(⋅∣st)[R(q,Fill(xt,a))],J_{t}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{s_{t}\sim d_{t}(q)}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})}\bigl[R\bigl(q,\textsc{Fill}(x_{t},a)\bigr)\bigr], (9)

where st=(q,xt)s_{t}=(q,x_{t}) and Fill​(xt,a)\textsc{Fill}(x_{t},a) deterministically completes xtx_{t} by filling its masked positions with aa.

Theorem 4.1 (Principled step-level policy gradient).

Assume (i) dt​(q)d_{t}(q) is independent of θ\theta, and (ii) π~θ(⋅∣s)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) is differentiable and normalized for each ss. Using the within-group mean baseline in Eq. 3, in the unclipped likelihood-ratio setting the expected gradient of the step-wise loss is aligned with the policy gradient of Jt​(θ)J_{t}(\theta):

𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep(t)​(θ)]=Z−1Z​∇θJt​(θ).\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(t)}(\theta)\bigr]=\frac{Z-1}{Z}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta). (10)

Proof idea. Write the step-wise loss (Eq. 5) as a score-function estimator for π~θ​(a∣st)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t}) using action-only log-probabilities on the current mask. The likelihood-ratio form gives the standard importance-weighted policy gradient; the within-group mean baseline induces only the constant factor (Z−1)/Z(Z-1)/Z in expectation and reduces variance. Full details are in Appendix A.1.

4.2 Mixed Objective and Overall Policy Gradient

A key property of DiSPO is that adding step-wise updates does not introduce an ad-hoc signal: in the unclipped, exact likelihood-ratio setting, the expected gradient of the combined loss (Eq. 8) equals the gradient of a single well-defined objective.

Terminal surrogate objective. Define the terminal (sequence-level) surrogate objective

Jseq(θ):=𝔼q∼𝒟,o∼π~θ(⋅∣q)[R(q,o)].J_{\text{seq}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\,o\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)}\bigl[R(q,o)\bigr]. (11)

A standard likelihood-ratio argument implies that the unclipped terminal loss ℒterm​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta) is an unbiased policy-gradient estimator for Jseq​(θ)J_{\text{seq}}(\theta) (Shao et al., 2024).

Mixed objective. Let cZ:=(Z−1)/Zc_{Z}:=(Z-1)/Z denote the constant scaling induced by the within-group mean baseline in Eq. 3. With timestep sampling ω⁡(t)\omega(t) and the step-wise objectives {Jt​(θ)}\{J_{t}(\theta)\} (Eq. 9), define

Jmix​(θ):=αstep​cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​Jt​(θ)+αterm​Jseq​(θ).J_{\text{mix}}(\theta):=\alpha_{\text{step}}\,c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\,J_{t}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\,J_{\text{seq}}(\theta). (12)
Theorem 4.2 (Overall policy gradient).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.1 (with the within-group mean baseline) and the standard likelihood-ratio assumptions for Jseq​(θ)J_{\text{seq}}(\theta),

𝔼⁡[−∇θℒ​(θ)]=∇θJmix​(θ),\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\bigr]=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{mix}}(\theta), (13)

where ℒ⁡(θ)=αstep​ℒstep​(θ)+αterm​ℒterm​(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\alpha_{\text{step}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta).

Proof idea. Condition on a timestep tt: Theorem 4.1 gives 𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep​(θ)∣t]=cZ​∇θJt​(θ)\mathbb{E}[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)\mid t]=c_{Z}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta). Averaging over t∼ω⁡(t)t\sim\omega(t) yields the step term cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​∇θJt​(θ)\;c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta). Then add 𝔼⁡[−∇θℒterm​(θ)]=∇θJseq​(θ)\mathbb{E}[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)]=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{seq}}(\theta) and use linearity of expectation. See Appendix A.2 for details.

4.3 Variance Reduction for the State-wise Estimator

DiSPO uses two simple mechanisms that reduce the variance of DiSPOś state-wise gradient estimates: (i) restricting gradients to actionable (masked) tokens, and (ii) averaging over ZZ candidates per state via cached-logit resampling.

Token-local updates. Fix a state s=(q,x)s=(q,x) of length LL with masked set MM of size m=|M|m=|M|, and let RR be the terminal reward of the resulting completion. Let gi:=∇θ​log​π~θ​(ai∣s,i)g_{i}:=\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{i}\mid s,i) denote a per-position score term. Compare an estimator that propagates through all positions, g^full:=∑i=1Lgi​R\hat{g}_{\text{full}}:=\sum_{i=1}^{L}g_{i}\,R, to the action-only estimator, g^sub:=∑i∈Mgi​R\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}:=\sum_{i\in M}g_{i}\,R.

Proposition 4.3 (Variance reduction by partial updates).

Assume {gi}\{g_{i}\} are independent, zero-mean with Var⁡[gi]=σ2\mathrm{Var}[g_{i}]=\sigma^{2}, and RR is independent of {gi}\{g_{i}\} with 𝔼⁡[R2]<∞\mathbb{E}[R^{2}]<\infty. Then

Var⁡[g^sub]≤mL​Var​[g^full].\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}]\leq\frac{m}{L}\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{full}}].

Proof idea. Under the assumptions, the variance of the sum scales linearly with the number of included positions, giving the factor m/Lm/L. See Appendix A.3.

Same-state averaging via cached-logit branching. At a fixed state ss, DiSPO can resample ZZ independent branches and average their gradient contributions. With any baseline b⁡(s)b(s) that is independent of each sampled action, the variance of the averaged estimator decreases at the standard O⁡(1/Z)O(1/Z) rate. Cached-logit branching avoids additional rollout forward passes to obtain these ZZ samples.

Proposition 4.4 (Variance vs. number of drafts).

Fix a state ss and draw i.i.d. actions a1,…,aZ∼π~θ(⋅∣s)a_{1},\dots,a_{Z}\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) with rewards RzR_{z}. Let b⁡(s)b(s) be any baseline independent of each aza_{z}, and define the per-branch contribution g^z:=(Rz−b⁡(s))​∇θ​log⁡π~θ​(az∣s)\hat{g}_{z}:=(R_{z}-b(s))\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{z}\mid s) with finite variance. Then the averaged estimator Var⁡[g^]=O⁡(1/Z)\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}]=O(1/Z).

Proof idea. The estimator is the average of ZZ i.i.d. per-branch terms under an action-independent baseline, so its variance shrinks by 1/Z1/Z. See Appendix A.4.

Remark (group-relative baseline used in practice). Our implementation uses the within-group mean baseline (Eq. 3), which introduces dependence across branches but typically further reduces variance in practice; we empirically verify variance reduction from increasing ZZ (§ 5).

5 Experiments

This section evaluates whether incorporating intermediate-state updates improves policy optimization for MDLMs. Since DiSPO naturally augments terminal-feedback optimization with a state-wise objective (Algo. 1; Eq. 18), we use the most direct baseline: diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b). To isolate the effect of state-conditioned credit assignment, we match training budgets by fixing i) the number of full diffusion rollouts, ii) the sequence-level group size, and iii) the number of RL update steps; DiSPO resamples by reusing cached-logit within each rollout.

5.1 Setup

Models. We evaluate LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) and a variant further fine-tuned on s1k (Muennighoff et al., 2025). Across methods, we follow the identical fine-tuning and RL recipe of Zhao et al. (2025b) and keep the denoising schedule fixed. See Appendix B.3 for more details.

Benchmarks and metrics. Following Zhao et al. (2025b), we report exact-match accuracy on benchmarks for math reasoning (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021); MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023)) and symbolic planning (Sudoku; Countdown (Zhao et al., 2025b)). See Appendix B.1 for details.

Optimization. For fair comparison, we match the baseline training setup across methods (including Ngen=256N_{\text{gen}}{=}256, denoising schedule, rollout budget, and the number of RL updates) and reuse the same terminal reward evaluator for both terminal and state-wise terms. Unless stated otherwise, DiSPO uses Z=2Z{=}2, samples one timestep per rollout from a late-biased polynomial distribution (degree k=4k{=}4), and sets αstep=0.1\alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.1; remaining hyperparameters are in Appendix B.3.

Evaluation. We follow the protocol of diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b). We evaluate at Ngen∈{128,256,512}N_{\text{gen}}\in\{128,256,512\} using zero-shot greedy decoding. For diffusion decoding, we use Ngen/2N_{\text{gen}}/2 denoising steps with a block size of 32 tokens. We provide more details in Appendix B.2.

5.2 Main results

Table 1 reports exact-match accuracy on four benchmarks for Ngen∈{128,256,512}N_{\text{gen}}\!\in\!\{128,256,512\}. At the default generation length (Ngen=256N_{\text{gen}}{=}256), DiSPO outperforms terminal-feedback diffu-GRPO across all model–benchmark pairs, with gains largely persisting at other generation lengths, including Avg.

Importantly, these gains are obtained under matched rollout forward passes and parameter-update steps, using the same terminal reward evaluator for both terminal and state-wise updates. This suggests the improvements come from finer-grained, state-wise credit assignment rather than extra rollouts or additional reward shaping.

To probe the underlying training dynamics, Fig. 2 plots both terminal rewards (top) and step rewards (bottom) on LLaDA-8B-Instruct. DiSPO reaches higher terminal rewards earlier and sustains them throughout training; while step rewards vary over a smaller range, they track the up and downs of terminal reward, consistent with a state-wise signal that aligns with terminal feedback along the trajectory.

5.3 Analysis: State-wise Estimator Design

Propositions 4.3 and 4.4 motivate two variance-reduction choices for intermediate-state policy optimization: (A) updating only actionable (newly filled) tokens and (B) averaging over ZZ same-state drafts. We evaluate both on 4×\times4 Sudoku via lightweight, controlled comparisons of step-wise gradient variance and task performance.

Empirical verification of gradient variance. To test the variance predictions, we measure the variance of the state-wise gradient estimator. At the last checkpoint for LLaDA-8B-Instruct in Sudoku, we repeatedly resample rollouts from the same set of states and estimate the trace covariance of the resulting state-wise gradient estimates, trCov⁡(g^)\mathrm{trCov}(\hat{g}). Figure 3 shows that (left) switching from all-token to actionable-token updates at Z=2Z{=}2 reduces trCov⁡(g^)\mathrm{trCov}(\hat{g}), and (right) increasing ZZ under actionable-only updates reduces it, consistent with Propositions 4.3 and 4.4 (Appendix C).

Impact on task performance. We then assess how these choices affect accuracy under the same training budget. Table 2 (top) shows that updating all tokens underperforms the actionable-only, supporting alignment with the state–action decomposition. Sweeping Z∈{2,3,4}Z\in\{2,3,4\} (bottom), we observe occasional gains at specific NgenN_{\text{gen}} but no monotonic improvement in average; we therefore use Z=2Z{=}2 by default.

5.4 Ablations: Optimization Recipe

We ablate three design choices for optimization: (i) which intermediate states to train on, (ii) the optimization objective, and (iii) weight for the step-wise objective (αstep\alpha_{\text{step}}).

Timestep sampling. We compare uniform sampling to polynomial samplers (k=4k{=}4) that bias draws toward late timesteps (near terminal states) or early timesteps (its mirrored variant). Table 3 (top) shows that late-biased sampling performs best, suggesting that very early masked states are too noisy for reliable credit assignment.

Objectives. Table 3 (middle) shows that ℒstep\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}} alone outperforms ℒterm\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}} alone, and combining them performs best, indicating complementary learning signals.

Intermediate-state weight. Table 3 (bottom) shows that, sweeping αstep∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\alpha_{\text{step}}\!\in\!\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}, performance consistently stays above αstep=0\alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0. However, gains are non-monotonic (best at αstep=0.5\alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.5), indicating its optimisation potential.

5.5 Error Analysis: Early Commitments

We analyze early-commitment errors using the final checkpoint of LLaD-8B-Instruct for Sudoku. We use Ngen=128N_{\text{gen}}{=}128; all other settings match the main experiments.

Figure 4 compares the same instance at the same denoising step: diffu-GRPO already violates constraints due to an early incorrect fill, whereas DiSPO maintains a consistent partial assignment. Figure 5 corroborates this at scale—the first-violation time occurs later with DiSPO. These indicate that state-wise optimization reduces premature, hard-to-correct commitments during denoising.

5.6 Compute Cost Breakdown

Algorithmic overhead. Table 4 shows per-prompt operation counts. DiSPO matches the dominant costs—diffusion-rollout forward passes (K​TKT) and optimizer updates (UU)—and adds only lightweight extras: reward evaluations for same-state branches and one-step surrogate calls to compute step-wise log-probs at selected states.

Wall-clock overhead and efficiency. Our current implementation is slower (∼\sim0.4×\times baseline throughput at Z=2Z{=}2 and |𝒮|=K|\mathcal{S}|{=}K), largely due to non-optimized repeated policy/surrogate calls and kernel/IO overhead; we discuss likely causes and optimizations in Appendix E. To account for this, Fig. 6 compares wall-clock-matched training curves: although DiSPO starts slower, it catches up and surpasses the terminal-feedback baseline within the same time budget, indicating improved performance per unit time from better credit assignment rather than extra rollout/update compute.

6 Related Work

Terminal-feedback policy optimization for MDLMs. Most RL fine-tuning methods for masked diffusion LMs use a scalar terminal reward on the final completion and perform PPO/GRPO-style updates via surrogate likelihoods (Zhao et al., 2025b; Tang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Rojas et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Zekri and Boullé, 2025; Zhao et al., 2025a). Our method differs by performing state-conditioned comparisons: at a fixed intermediate state, we contrast alternative mask fillings (actions) rather than only learning from terminal rollouts.

State-aware reward shaping. SAPO scores intermediate denoising states to build step-aware bonuses that shape the terminal signal (Xie et al., 2025), typically requiring additional multi-step rollouts. In contrast, DiSPO directory optimizes intermediate-state actions without extra rollouts; a reference comparison is provided in Appendix D.

Trajectory-level objectives. MDPO aligns with the denoising trajectory by comparing different rollouts across steps and favoring trajectories whose intermediate predictions improve toward the terminal outcome (He et al., 2025). In contrast, DiSPO uses a different optimization unit: it fixes an intermediate state and compares alternative mask fillings.

Surrogate likelihoods and gradient estimators. Complementary work improves surrogate likelihoods or policy-gradient estimators for diffusion LMs (Wang et al., 2025a; Zekri and Boullé, 2025; Rojas et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). DiSPO can directly incorporate improved surrogates/estimators while keeping the state-wise objective unchanged.

7 Conclusion

We propose DiSPO, a plug-in intermediate-state credit-assignment layer for policy optimization of masked diffusion language models, grounded in a policy-gradient formulation (§ 3). This formulation induces step-wise and mixed objectives with principled policy-gradient estimators, and we analyze its variance reduction mechanisms (§ 4). Empirically, instantiating DiSPO on top of terminal-feedback diffu-GRPO, we consistently improve accuracy across math and planning tasks under matched rollout forward passes and update steps using the same terminal reward (§ 5).

Limitations and discussion. DiSPO is a plug-in state-wise credit-assignment layer; future work includes pairing it with other terminal-feedback objectives (e.g., GDPO (Rojas et al., 2025)) and improved surrogate likelihood or gradient estimators (e.g., SPG (Wang et al., 2025a)). We also use an unshaped terminal reward; studying complementarity with reward shaping (e.g., SAPO (Xie et al., 2025)) would clarify their interaction.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning by improving policy optimization for masked diffusion language models. There are many potential societal consequences of improved language-model reasoning capabilities, including both beneficial applications and possible misuse; we do not believe our method introduces unique ethical concerns beyond those common to this line of research.

𝔼[1Z∑z=1ZR¯∇θlogπ~θ(az∣sk,t)]=1Z𝔼a∼π~θ(⋅∣sk,t)[ℛ(sk,t,a)∇θlogπ~θ(a∣sk,t)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\bar{R}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{z}\mid s_{k,t})\right]=\frac{1}{Z}\,\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{k,t})}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(s_{k,t},a)\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a\mid s_{k,t})\bigr].

Therefore,

𝔼[−∇θℒstep(k,t)(θ)∣q,sk,t]=Z−1Z𝔼a∼π~θ(⋅∣sk,t)[ℛ(sk,t,a)∇θlogπ~θ(a∣sk,t)].\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(k,t)}(\theta)\mid q,s_{k,t}\bigr]=\frac{Z-1}{Z}\,\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{k,t})}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(s_{k,t},a)\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a\mid s_{k,t})\bigr].

Taking outer expectations over q∼𝒟q\sim\mathcal{D} and sk,t∼dt​(q)s_{k,t}\sim d_{t}(q) yields

𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep(t)​(θ)]=Z−1Z​∇θJt​(θ),\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(t)}(\theta)\bigr]=\frac{Z-1}{Z}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta),

which matches Theorem 4.1. ∎

Remark on the group baseline. If a leave-one-out baseline is used (independent of each branch action), the estimator is unbiased. With the within-group mean baseline in Eq. 3 used in our implementation, the expected gradient is scaled by the constant factor (Z−1)/Z(Z-1)/Z, which can be absorbed into αstep\alpha_{\text{step}} or the learning rate.

A.2 Proof of Theorem 4.2

We prove that the expected gradient of the combined loss equals the gradient of the mixed objective. Throughout, we treat the masked-token surrogate π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} as the policy being optimized and work in the unclipped setting stated in §4.2.

Recall the mixed objective and combined loss. Let cZ:=(Z−1)/Zc_{Z}:=(Z-1)/Z denote the constant scaling induced by the within-group mean baseline in the step-wise estimator. The mixed objective (Eq. 12) is

Jmix​(θ)=αstep​cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​Jt​(θ)+αterm​Jseq​(θ),J_{\text{mix}}(\theta)=\alpha_{\text{step}}\,c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\,J_{t}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\,J_{\text{seq}}(\theta),

where Jt​(θ)J_{t}(\theta) is the step-wise objective (Eq. 9) and Jseq​(θ)J_{\text{seq}}(\theta) is the terminal surrogate objective (Eq. 11). The combined training loss is

ℒ⁡(θ)=αstep​ℒstep​(θ)+αterm​ℒterm​(θ).\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\alpha_{\text{step}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta).

By linearity of differentiation,

∇θJmix​(θ)=αstep​cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​∇θJt​(θ)+αterm​∇θJseq​(θ).\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{mix}}(\theta)=\alpha_{\text{step}}\,c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{seq}}(\theta). (18)

It therefore suffices to show that 𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep​(θ)]=cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​∇θJt​(θ)\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)\right]=c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta) and 𝔼⁡[−∇θℒterm​(θ)]=∇θJseq​(θ).\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)\right]=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{seq}}(\theta).

Step term. Recall that ℒstep​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta) is computed by selecting timesteps according to ω⁡(t)\omega(t) and applying the per-state step loss ℒstep(k,t)​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(k,t)}(\theta) (Eq. 5) on the corresponding intermediate state(s). Condition on a particular timestep tt being selected. Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.1, we have

𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep​(θ)|t]=cZ​∇θJt​(θ),\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)\,\middle|\,t\right]=c_{Z}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta),

where the expectation is over q∼𝒟q\sim\mathcal{D}, st∼dt​(q)s_{t}\sim d_{t}(q), and the branched action samples at that state. Taking expectation over t∼ω⁡(t)t\sim\omega(t) yields

𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep​(θ)]=cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​∇θJt​(θ).\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)\right]=c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta). (19)

Terminal term. By definition,

Jseq(θ)=𝔼q∼𝒟𝔼o∼π~θ(⋅∣q)[R(q,o)].J_{\text{seq}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{o\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)}\bigl[R(q,o)\bigr].

A standard score-function (REINFORCE) argument gives

∇θJseq​(θ)=𝔼q,o∼π~θ​[R⁡(q,o)​∇θ​log⁡π~θ​(o∣q)],\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{seq}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q,o\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}}\bigl[R(q,o)\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(o\mid q)\bigr],

and subtracting any baseline that depends on qq but not on oo preserves unbiasedness. The terminal GRPO loss ℒterm​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta) is precisely the corresponding baseline-centered (and, in practice, importance-weighted) estimator; in the unclipped setting,

𝔼⁡[−∇θℒterm​(θ)]=∇θJseq​(θ),\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)\right]=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{seq}}(\theta), (20)

which is the standard PPO/GRPO identity (see, e.g., Shao et al. (2024)).

Combine the terms. Combining Eq. 19 and Eq. 20 and using linearity of expectation,

𝔼⁡[−∇θℒ​(θ)]=αstep​cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​∇θJt​(θ)+αterm​∇θJseq​(θ)=∇θJmix​(θ),\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right]=\alpha_{\text{step}}\,c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{seq}}(\theta)=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{mix}}(\theta),

where the last equality follows from Eq. 18 with the definition of Jmix​(θ)J_{\text{mix}}(\theta) above. This proves Theorem 4.2. ∎

Remark (KL-regularized case). If the main text includes a KL penalty, the same argument applies after adding the term −λ𝔼q[KL(π~θ(⋅∣q)∥π~ref(⋅∣q))]-\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{q}[\mathrm{KL}(\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\,\|\,\tilde{\pi}_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid q))] to Jmix​(θ)J_{\text{mix}}(\theta) and the corresponding penalty λ​ℒKL​(θ)\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}(\theta) to ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta); differentiation under the expectation yields the additional gradient term.

A.3 Proof of Proposition 4.3

We prove the variance reduction claim for the token-local (action-only) estimator under the stated independence assumptions.

Setup. Fix a diffusion state s=(q,x)s=(q,x) of length LL with masked set M⊆[L]M\subseteq[L] of size m=|M|m=|M|. Let RR denote the (scalar) terminal reward associated with the filled candidate, and define per-position score terms

gi:=∇θ​log​π~θ​(ai∣s,i),g_{i}\;:=\;\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{i}\mid s,i),

where aia_{i} is the token sampled at position ii (for i∈Mi\in M) and π~θ(⋅∣s,i)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s,i) is the one-step surrogate distribution at position ii. Consider the two estimators (as in §4.3)

g^full=∑i=1Lgi​R,g^sub=∑i∈Mgi​R.\hat{g}_{\text{full}}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{L}g_{i}\,R,\qquad\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}\;=\;\sum_{i\in M}g_{i}\,R.

Variance calculation. Under the assumptions of Proposition 4.3, {gi}i=1L\{g_{i}\}_{i=1}^{L} are independent, zero-mean with Var⁡[gi]=σ2\mathrm{Var}[g_{i}]=\sigma^{2}, and RR is independent of all gig_{i} with 𝔼⁡[R2]<∞\mathbb{E}[R^{2}]<\infty. First, independence across positions implies

Var⁡[∑i∈Sgi​R]=∑i∈SVar⁡[gi​R]for any index set ​S⊆[L].\mathrm{Var}\!\left[\sum_{i\in S}g_{i}R\right]=\sum_{i\in S}\mathrm{Var}[g_{i}R]\quad\text{for any index set }S\subseteq[L].

Second, since gig_{i} is independent of RR and 𝔼⁡[gi]=0\mathbb{E}[g_{i}]=0,

Var⁡[gi​R]=𝔼⁡[gi2​R2]−(𝔼⁡[gi​R])2=𝔼⁡[gi2]​𝔼​[R2]=σ2​𝔼​[R2].\mathrm{Var}[g_{i}R]=\mathbb{E}[g_{i}^{2}R^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[g_{i}R])^{2}=\mathbb{E}[g_{i}^{2}]\mathbb{E}[R^{2}]=\sigma^{2}\,\mathbb{E}[R^{2}].

Therefore,

Var⁡[g^full]=∑i=1Lσ2​𝔼​[R2]=L​σ2​𝔼​[R2],Var⁡[g^sub]=∑i∈Mσ2​𝔼​[R2]=m​σ2​𝔼​[R2].\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{full}}]=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}[R^{2}]=L\,\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}[R^{2}],\qquad\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}]=\sum_{i\in M}\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}[R^{2}]=m\,\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}[R^{2}].

Taking the ratio yields

Var⁡[g^sub]=mL​Var​[g^full],\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}]=\frac{m}{L}\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{full}}],

which implies the stated inequality in Proposition 4.3 since m≤Lm\leq L. ∎

Remark (vector-valued gradients). If each gig_{i} is vector-valued, the same argument applies coordinate-wise. Equivalently, writing tr​Cov​[⋅]\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}[\cdot] for the trace of the covariance matrix, independence implies tr​Cov​[g^sub]=mL​tr​Cov​[g^full]\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}[\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}]=\frac{m}{L}\,\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}[\hat{g}_{\text{full}}] under the same assumptions.

A.4 Proof of Proposition 4.4

We prove the O⁡(1/Z)O(1/Z) variance reduction from averaging ZZ (approximately) independent branches at a fixed state.

Setup. Fix a state ss and draw i.i.d. actions a1,…,aZ∼π~θ(⋅∣s)a_{1},\dots,a_{Z}\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) with associated rewards RzR_{z}. Let b⁡(s)b(s) be any baseline independent of each sampled action aza_{z}, and define the per-branch contribution

g^z:=(Rz−b⁡(s))​∇θ​log⁡π~θ​(az∣s).\hat{g}_{z}\;:=\;(R_{z}-b(s))\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{z}\mid s).

Define the averaged estimator

g^:=1Z​∑z=1Zg^z,\hat{g}\;:=\;\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\hat{g}_{z},

and assume g^z\hat{g}_{z} have finite variance.

Variance of an average. For the scalar case, independence gives

Var⁡[g^]=Var⁡[1Z​∑z=1Zg^z]=1Z2​∑z=1ZVar⁡[g^z]=1Z​Var​[g^z],\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}]=\mathrm{Var}\!\left[\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\hat{g}_{z}\right]=\frac{1}{Z^{2}}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{z}]=\frac{1}{Z}\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{z}],

where Var⁡[g^z]\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{z}] is the same for all zz since {g^z}z=1Z\{\hat{g}_{z}\}_{z=1}^{Z} are i.i.d. Thus Var⁡[g^]=O⁡(1/Z)\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}]=O(1/Z).

For the vector-valued case, the same argument holds for covariance matrices. Under independence,

Cov⁡[g^]=Cov⁡[1Z​∑z=1Zg^z]=1Z2​∑z=1ZCov⁡[g^z]=1Z​Cov​[g^z],\mathrm{Cov}[\hat{g}]=\mathrm{Cov}\!\left[\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\hat{g}_{z}\right]=\frac{1}{Z^{2}}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\mathrm{Cov}[\hat{g}_{z}]=\frac{1}{Z}\,\mathrm{Cov}[\hat{g}_{z}],

where the last equality uses that {g^z}z=1Z\{\hat{g}_{z}\}_{z=1}^{Z} are i.i.d. and hence have identical covariance. Therefore tr​Cov​[g^]=1Z​tr​Cov​[g^z]=O⁡(1/Z)\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}[\hat{g}]=\frac{1}{Z}\,\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}[\hat{g}_{z}]=O(1/Z). ∎

Remark (group-relative baseline used in practice). Our implementation uses the within-group mean baseline (Eq. 3), which introduces dependence across branches. Proposition 4.4 formalizes the standard 1/Z1/Z reduction for action-independent baselines; empirically, increasing ZZ reduces variance in our setting as well (§ 5).

Appendix B Experimental Details

This appendix provides additional details on benchmarks, reward functions, and training/implementation settings used in our experiments. We follow the d1/diffu-GRPO recipe wherever applicable (Zhao et al., 2025b); in particular, our SFT procedure and programmatic reward evaluators are reused from d1. Exact run-specific hyperparameters (including optimizer schedules, seeds, and infrastructure settings) are recorded in the configuration files of our code scheduled for release.

B.1 Benchmarks, Evaluation Protocol, and Reward Functions

We evaluate on four reasoning benchmarks following Zhao et al. (2025b). For each task, we report exact-match accuracy and use a programmatic verifier to compute a scalar reward R⁡(q,o)R(q,o) from the model completion oo given prompt qq. Unless stated otherwise, rewards are binary (11 for a valid correct solution and 00 otherwise), and DiSPO applies the same terminal reward function for both the sequence-level and state-wise objectives, i.e., non-reward shaping on terminal rewards and non-custom engineering for step-wise rewards. For fully fair comparison, implementations for the reward functions are reused from diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b) without modification i.e., https://github.com/dllm-reasoning/d1.

GSM8K. GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) is a grade-school math word-problem benchmark. It uses exact match on the final numeric answer after applying the same answer-extraction and normalization rules. We use the training data publicly available https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k. Reward is computed by considering multiple axes, i.e., format reward (max. 1.6251.625) and correctness reward (max. 2.02.0).

MATH500. MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023) is a subset of MATH focusing on competition-level problems. Reward is computed by considering the two axes, i.e., format reward (max 1.01.0) and correctness reward (max 2.02.0)

Sudoku. 4×\times4 Sudoku tasks is synthetic benchmark for planning. We use the training data publicly available https://github.com/Black-Phoenix/4x4-Sudoku-Dataset. As for the evaluation data, we use the synthetically created problem set by using specific implementation https://www.ocf.berkeley.edu/~arel/sudoku/main.html. Reward is the fraction of empty cells filled correctly.

Countdown. Countdown is an arithmetic-planning benchmark, whose training data publicly available https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4. Evaluation parses the output into an arithmetic expression, verifies that it uses the provided numbers under the task rules, and checks that the expression evaluates exactly to the target value. Reward is computed by considering the two axes, i.e., nearly-correct answers obtain 0.10.1 and the perfect answers gain 1.01.0.

B.2 Inference Details

For inference, we use semi-autoregressive decoding with 32-token blocks (Arriola et al., 2025), unmasking the 2 highest-confidence tokens per step within each block. We evaluate at Ngen∈{128,256,512}N_{\text{gen}}\in\{128,256,512\} using zero-shot prompting and greedy decoding.

B.3 Training and Implementation Details

Model variants and SFT. We evaluate two model variants: (1) LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025), and (2) its variant additionally fine-tuned on the s1k dataset (Muennighoff et al., 2025). Across algorithms, we use the same SFT recipe for each model variant (data, schedule, and hyperparameters), reusing the d1 implementation where applicable; https://github.com/dllm-reasoning/d1. We keep the architecture, tokenizer, and denoising schedule fixed throughout. Furthermore, to isolate the effect of state-wise updates, we match compute-relevant quantities across methods, including: the number of RL update steps (3800/5000/7700/6600 steps for Sudoku/Countdown/GSM8K/MATH500, respectively). These are often task-dependent. Please refer to their experimental configuration.

DiSPO-specific settings. Unless stated otherwise, DiSPO uses a conservative default settings. Concretely, we set branch size Z=2Z{=}2 completion candidates per selected intermediate state with a timestep-sampling distribution q⁡(t)q(t) for selecting intermediate time steps (§ 5), with polynomial exponent k=4k{=}4, and loss weights αstep=0.1\alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.1 and αterm=1\alpha_{\text{term}}{=}1. We additionally specify the number of selected timesteps per trajectory |Tsub|=1|T_{\text{sub}}|{=}1 for light-weight evaluation.

Optimization. Following Zhao et al. (2025b), we use LoRA with a rank r=128r=128 and scaling factor α=64\alpha=64, and AdamW optimizer ( , ). We basically set hyperparameters as follows: β1=0.9,β2=0.99\beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.99, weight decay 0.10.1, learning rate 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}, gradient clipping 0.20.2. We train on 44 NVIDIA H100-94G GPUs with batch size 6 per GPU, gradient accumulation steps of 4, and sequence length of 256 tokens.

Appendix C Empirical Measurement of Step-level Gradient Variance

We detail the protocol used to produce Fig. 3, which measures the variance of the step-level gradient estimator via repeated same-state branching.

Quantity measured. Fix an intermediate diffusion state s=(q,x)s=(q,x) and draft size ZZ. Let ℒstep​(s,θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(s;\theta) denote the unclipped per-state step loss obtained by instantiating Eq. 5 at state ss with ZZ same-state branches, using the state-wise surrogate log-probability (Eq. 4) and group advantages (Eq. 3). We define the step-level gradient estimator as the update direction

g^step​(s):=−∇θℒstep​(s,θ)∈ℝd,\hat{g}_{\text{step}}(s)\;:=\;-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(s;\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

We summarize the variance of this random vector by the trace covariance

trCov⁡(g^step​(s)):=tr⁡(Cov⁡[g^step​(s)])=𝔼⁡[‖g^step​(s)‖2]−‖𝔼⁡[g^step​(s)]‖2.\mathrm{trCov}\bigl(\hat{g}_{\text{step}}(s)\bigr):=\mathrm{tr}\!\left(\mathrm{Cov}\bigl[\hat{g}_{\text{step}}(s)\bigr]\right)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\hat{g}_{\text{step}}(s)\|^{2}\right]-\left\|\mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{g}_{\text{step}}(s)\right]\right\|^{2}.

Empirically, for each fixed state ss we repeat same-state branching RR times to obtain {g^step(r)​(s)}r=1R\{\hat{g}^{(r)}_{\text{step}}(s)\}_{r=1}^{R} and estimate

trCov^​(g^step​(s))=1R−1​∑r=1R‖g^step(r)​(s)−g¯step​(s)‖2,g¯step​(s)=1R​∑r=1Rg^step(r)​(s).\widehat{\mathrm{trCov}}\bigl(\hat{g}_{\text{step}}(s)\bigr)=\frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\left\|\hat{g}^{(r)}_{\text{step}}(s)-\bar{g}_{\text{step}}(s)\right\|^{2},\qquad\bar{g}_{\text{step}}(s)=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\hat{g}^{(r)}_{\text{step}}(s).

Task, checkpoint, and state collection. We run this diagnostic on 4×\times4 Sudoku for efficiency and use a fixed model checkpoint from DiSPO training (LLaDA optimized with DiSPO; step-3800). We collect intermediate states from 64 prompts and sample 8 states per prompt, yielding 512 candidate states.

State filtering and paired aggregation. To ensure a fair comparison across different conditions (e.g., different ZZ and action-only vs full-token updates), we fix the same state set for all conditions and retain only non-degenerate states; at the state (i) at least one actionable token contributes to the step loss (denominator >0>0), and (ii) among the RR repeated branchings, at least one trial yields an advantage >0>0. After filtering, we aggregate trCov^​(g^step​(s))\widehat{\mathrm{trCov}}(\hat{g}_{\text{step}}(s)) over 276 states.

Compared settings. Z=2Z=2 with action-only updates is the default setting used in our main experiments (Table 1); Including that, for the ZZ ablation, we test Z∈{2,3,4}Z\in\{2,3,4\}; for the update-target ablation, we test the full-tokens and action-only variants. Bars in Fig. 3 show the difference in gradient variance from the default (Z=2Z=2, action-only), with error bars indicating paired 95% bootstrap CIs over states.

Appendix D Reference Comparison with Step-Aware Terminal Reward Shaping

Difference in objectives. SAPO (Xie et al., 2025) and DiSPO both leverage intermediate diffusion states, but they do so for different purposes. SAPO scores intermediate states to shape the terminal rewards, whereas DiSPO directly optimizes intermediate-state actions—the mask fillings sampled at a fixed partially-masked state—by comparing same-state counterfactual fillings under the unchanged terminal reward. Hence, the two approaches are best viewed as complementary.

Difference in compute. This difference in design also leads to substantially different compute profiles. As summarized in Table 5, DiSPO adds overhead mainly through extra reward evaluations for same-state branches and one-step surrogate evaluations for step-wise log-probabilities, while matching diffusion-rollout forward passes and update steps. In contrast, SAPO typically incurs additional multi-step continuation rollouts from intermediate states to estimate shaping terms, which increases the dominant cost—diffusion-rollout forward passes—often by a large margin. Therefore, SAPO is not only complementary in approach, but can also be considerably more expensive in required rollout compute.

Reference comparison in benchmarks. Despite the mismatch in objectives and compute, SAPO is a representative step-aware method, so we include a reference comparison to contextualize DiSPO. This comparison should be interpreted with caution: the methods optimize different training signals (shaped vs. unshaped terminal rewards) and can require very different rollout compute (Table 5), so the evaluation is not an apples-to-apples matched-budget study. To keep this reference study lightweight, we report results on two representative benchmarks from our main suite: Sudoku (planning) and MATH500 (math), sweeping αstep∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\alpha_{\text{step}}\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}. Table 6 reports that, in 11/12 settings, DiSPO outperforms SAPO, despite using substantially less rollout compute.

Takeaway. These results suggest that, among ways to leverage intermediate diffusion states, directly optimizing intermediate mask-filling actions can be a particularly effective alternative to using intermediate-state scores only for reward shaping, achieving competitive performance at a fraction of the rollout compute. At the same time, since SAPO and DiSPO act on different axes (reward shaping vs. action-level optimization), they are potentially complementary; we leave a careful study of joint training recipes to future work.

Appendix E Discussion on the Wall-clock Overhead

Observed overhead. In our current implementation, DiSPO runs at lower throughput than the terminal-feedback baseline (reported in §5.6) even at modest settings (e.g., Z=2Z{=}2). This slowdown reflects engineering overhead rather than additional rollout/update compute, since the dominant algorithmic costs (K​TKT rollout forward passes and UU updates) are matched.

Likely causes. The main contributors are repeated, non-amortized calls: (i) evaluating multiple same-state branches and (ii) computing step-wise log-probs via one-step surrogate calls at selected states. When executed largely sequentially, these introduce frequent kernel launches, synchronization points, and host-side overhead that can dominate wall-clock time despite modest extra FLOPs.

Optimization opportunities. These costs are not intrinsic to the method and should be reducible by (1) batching same-state branches (amortizing policy/surrogate/reward calls over ZZ), (2) caching state representations for step-wise terms, and (3) reducing kernel/IO overhead (e.g., call fusion / compilation and fewer synchronization points). We therefore, as a reference, additionally reported wall-clock-matched curves (Fig. 6) to ensure the performance gains (rewards and accuracy) are robust to current implementation overheads.
